reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: CVID is the most common symptomatic primary antibody deficiency and typically presents in adolescence or adulthood with recurrent sinopulmonary infections by encapsulated bacteria
The hallmark is low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM plus a poor antibody response to vaccines, in the absence of another defined cause of hypogammaglobulinaemia

It is far more than an infection disorder: autoimmune cytopenias, granulomatous disease, enteropathy, lymphoid hyperplasia, and an increased risk of lymphoma are common and drive much of the morbidity
Diagnosis is often delayed for years, so recurrent bacterial infections or unexplained bronchiectasis in an adult should prompt measurement of immunoglobulins
Bronchiectasis from repeated or inadequately treated infection is a leading cause of chronic morbidity, making early recognition and airway surveillance important
The mainstay of treatment is immunoglobulin replacement, given intravenously or subcutaneously, titrated to reduce infection frequency
Live vaccines should generally be avoided and are unreliable, and antibody responses to immunisation are used diagnostically rather than for protection
Autoimmune and inflammatory complications may need immunosuppression, which must be balanced carefully against the underlying immune deficiency
Because it is a heterogeneous diagnosis of exclusion, secondary causes such as protein loss, drugs, and haematologic malignancy must be ruled out
reference.pathophysiology: CVID is a heterogeneous group of primary immunodeficiencies characterised by defective differentiation of B cells into immunoglobulin-secreting plasma cells and impaired class switching and memory B-cell formation, resulting in low serum immunoglobulins and failure of specific antibody responses. Although predominantly a humoral defect, many patients also have T-cell and innate immune abnormalities and dysregulated immune tolerance, which explain the frequent autoimmune and granulomatous-lymphoproliferative complications. Most cases are sporadic; a minority carry identifiable monogenic defects (e.g. in TACI/TNFRSF13B, ICOS, CD19 complex, NFKB pathways). The combined immune dysfunction predisposes to both infection and immune dysregulation, including malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia from drugs (e.g. rituximab, anticonvulsants) or protein loss
X-linked agammaglobulinaemia and other defined primary antibody deficiencies
Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, lymphoma, or myeloma causing immunoglobulin deficiency
Specific antibody deficiency with normal immunoglobulin levels
HIV infection and protein-losing states (nephrotic syndrome, enteropathy)
additionalInvestigations: Serum IgG, IgA, and IgM with IgG subclasses
Specific antibody titres before and after protein and polysaccharide vaccination
Lymphocyte subset and B-cell memory phenotyping
Exclusion of secondary causes (serum protein electrophoresis, HIV, drug review, urinary protein)
Chest imaging (including CT) for bronchiectasis and lung disease
Targeted biopsy and genetic testing when complications or a monogenic cause are suspected
redFlags: Severe or overwhelming bacterial infection or sepsis in an untreated antibody-deficient patient
Rapidly enlarging lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or systemic symptoms suggesting lymphoma
Progressive respiratory decline from bronchiectasis or interstitial lung disease
Severe autoimmune cytopenia or refractory enteropathy causing haemodynamic or nutritional compromise
reference.prognosis: With regular immunoglobulin replacement and prompt treatment of infection, life expectancy has improved substantially. Prognosis is worst in patients who develop non-infectious complications-bronchiectasis, chronic lung disease, autoimmune disease, granulomatous-lymphoproliferative disease, and lymphoma-which are now the main determinants of mortality.
pitfalls: Delaying diagnosis by not measuring immunoglobulins in adults with recurrent sinopulmonary infection or unexplained bronchiectasis
Attributing autoimmune or granulomatous complications to a separate disease rather than to CVID itself
Giving live vaccines or relying on vaccination for protection in an antibody-deficient patient
Failing to exclude secondary and malignant causes of hypogammaglobulinaemia before labelling CVID
management: Immunoglobulin replacement (intravenous or subcutaneous), titrated against the trough level and infection frequency, is the mainstay of therapy
Treat bacterial infections promptly and with a low threshold, and consider prophylactic antibiotics in those with frequent sinopulmonary infection
Institute airway clearance, chest physiotherapy and early antibiotic treatment of exacerbations to preserve lung function and limit progression of bronchiectasis
Treat autoimmune cytopenias and granulomatous-lymphoproliferative disease with corticosteroids, rituximab or other immunosuppression under specialist guidance
Avoid live vaccines and instead give inactivated vaccines, recognising that antibody responses may be poor
Undertake structured surveillance with lung imaging, blood counts and vigilance for lymphoma and chronic lung disease
Manage through clinical immunology, with genetic testing when a monogenic cause or transplant candidacy is being considered
